medical.title: Understanding adult obesity
medical.summary: Obesity is one of the most common health conditions in the world and one of the most misunderstood. Today, it affects about 4 in 10 U.S. adults, and the numbers keep rising.

medical.title: ASTRO: Low-dose radiotherapy shows potential in early knee osteoarthritis
medical.summary: Low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) offers multiple benefits in early knee osteoarthritis (OA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Society for Radiation Oncology, held from Sept. 26 to 30 in Boston.

medical.title: Scientists uncover two-pronged strategy to overcome glioblastoma's resistance to immunotherapy
medical.summary: Scientists at The Wistar Institute have identified a combination treatment that overcomes two of the biggest barriers to immunotherapy in glioblastoma. In a study published in Neuro-Oncology, the researchers show that reprogramming myeloid cells, a type of immune cell that glioblastoma tumors co-opt to protect themselves, while simultaneously boosting cancer-fighting T cells shrank the tumors and prevented them from coming back.

medical.title: The importance of peer support following a termination of pregnancy for medical reasons
medical.summary: The first study exploring women's experiences of peer support following a termination for medical reasons (TFMR) highlights the profound isolation, misunderstanding and stigma women experience and the importance of peer support.

medical.title: Hospital closures on the rise in both rural and urban areas—particularly among safety-net hospitals
medical.summary: More hospitals across the U.S. are closing than opening, and urban hospitals are closing at the same rate as rural ones, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Further, the hospitals that close are more likely to be those serving socially vulnerable communities.

medical.title: Life-course clinical obesity linked to signs of brain health changes in midlife
medical.summary: New research from the Bogalusa Heart Study has found that greater exposure to clinical obesity during young adulthood is associated with a greater burden of white matter changes in the brain by midlife, providing new insight into how metabolic health across the life span may influence brain health.

medical.title: Allergic to gold jewelry? Lab tests reveal gold can dissolve from earrings under specific chemical conditions
medical.summary: Gold has a reputation for being chemically untouchable. But according to Western University chemist Yolanda Hedberg, that reputation is a little misleading—gold is not unreactive so much as selective about what it reacts with.

medical.title: Human milk offers a window into mammary gland function—and its links to infant growth
medical.summary: A study led by researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine identified shared molecular patterns in human milk that link maternal nutrition, mammary gland biology and infant growth.

medical.title: Polynesian wayfinding is written in the genomes of island populations
medical.summary: For centuries, Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean, using their knowledge of stars, currents, birds, clouds and the sea to settle islands across the Pacific. Now, a new University of California San Diego study shows the history of voyaging is also reflected in the genomes of Polynesian populations today.

medical.title: Thinking of taking melatonin to help you sleep? Here's what you need to know
medical.summary: Whether you're struggling with jet lag, working shifts and sleeping during the day, or dealing with more severe insomnia, you might have wondered if melatonin can help you get better sleep.

medical.title: PrEP pill can prevent HIV, but partner reactions might stand in the way
medical.summary: Fear of accusations of infidelity, the stigma surrounding HIV and concerns about causing conflict in a relationship might deter some Black women from using PrEP, a prescription medicine used to prevent HIV, according to a study led by Rutgers researchers.

medical.title: More men living longer with incurable prostate cancer, report finds
medical.summary: Men in England diagnosed with incurable advanced prostate cancer are more likely to survive for at least three years than they were a decade ago, according to an analysis by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and partners.

medical.title: How political upheaval and the pandemic shaped UK mental health
medical.summary: Major societal events such as the Brexit referendum and COVID-19 lockdowns have contributed to a lasting deterioration in mental health in the U.K., a study led by University College London (UCL) researchers finds.

medical.title: Personality data reveal link between neuroticism and lasting pandemic anxiety and depression
medical.summary: An individual's personality, especially how strongly they react to uncertainty, may help indicate how vulnerable they are to prolonged mental distress during a major crisis, according to a new USC-led study.

medical.title: Common herbal sleep aid shows signs of addictive potential
medical.summary: Cannabinol is a popular ingredient in over-the-counter sleep products, marketed as a gentle, plant-derived way to unwind at the end of the day. But new research conducted at the University of Connecticut suggests consumers should use it with caution.

medical.title: Randomized trial finds targeting individual metastases in oligometastatic breast cancer does not improve survival
medical.summary: Treating individual metastatic tumors with highly focused radiation or surgery did not improve progression-free or overall survival for patients with oligometastatic breast cancer receiving first-line systemic therapy, according to results from the randomized NRG-BR002 clinical trial led by researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

medical.title: Long-running women's health studies reveal lasting lessons for disease prevention and healthy aging
medical.summary: Andrea Romanos-Nanclares, Ph.D., of the Channing Division of Network Medicine within the Department of Medicine at Mass General Brigham, is the lead author of a paper published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health titled "The Nurses' Health Studies: a half-century of discovery in women's health." A. Heather Eliassen, ScD, of Mass General Brigham and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, is the senior author.

medical.title: Cervical cancer trial finds similar early recovery results after robot-assisted versus open surgery
medical.summary: In early-stage cervical cancer, radical hysterectomy is an established treatment. The operation can be performed either through open surgery or robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery. Until now, there have been limited data from large randomized studies on differences in complications and recovery between the methods.

medical.title: Public dataset aims to teach AI to 'show its work' on CT scans
medical.summary: Earlier this summer, an international team led by biomedical informatics researchers at Harvard Medical School released the first public dataset that connects descriptive radiological information, such as "3 mm nodule in the lower left lobe," to precise locations in chest CT scans.

medical.title: How a new long-acting HIV drug combo tackles resistance
medical.summary: A new long-acting HIV treatment could expand options for people who have trouble taking daily pills and whose virus is resistant to some commonly used HIV drugs, according to a new UC San Francisco study.

medical.title: New genetic insights could help detect hearing loss earlier
medical.summary: A team of hearing specialists at Vanderbilt Health analyzed thousands of data samples in the institution's BioVU biobank to understand genetic susceptibility of sensorineural hearing loss, which is caused by damage to the inner ear. Their study is published in JAMA Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery.

medical.title: Ancient viral DNA helps embryonic stem cells grow—and cancer hijacks the same switch
medical.summary: Three years ago, George Kassiotis and his team made an unexpected discovery: A specific way of producing a protein called calbindin was found to help cancer cells survive by preventing them from aging. This left Kassiotis, who runs the Crick's Retroviral Immunology Laboratory, confused. Why would a mechanism that boosts cancer growth exist in the first place?

medical.title: Scientists outline blueprint for next-generation wearable eye health sensors
medical.summary: Dr. Yangzhi Zhu of the Terasaki Institute for Biomedical Innovation (TIBI), with collaborators at UC San Diego and USC, published a Nature Sensors perspective on what it will take to turn tear-based wearable sensors into reliable, long-term health-tracking tools.

medical.title: Traumatic brain injury can alter the brain's subsequent response to stress, study shows
medical.summary: Researchers from the Department of Cell Biology, Genetics and Physiology at the University of Malaga have led an international scientific team studying how a traumatic brain injury caused by a severe blow to the head affects the brain's long-term response to subsequent stressful situations.

medical.title: Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice
medical.summary: Just seven strength-training sessions helped obese mice shrink visceral fat cells and reactivate molecular pathways involved in burning stored fat, despite no change in overall body weight. The findings suggest some benefits of resistance exercise may begin long before weight loss becomes visible, though the results still need to be confirmed in humans.

science.title: Study shows how children learn to talk about characters' thoughts and feelings in stories
science.summary: An international research effort has examined how children develop the ability to express what story characters think, feel and perceive. Research groups from around the world collected 5,507 picture-based stories from 2,763 typically developing monolingual and bilingual children ages 3 to 13. The children came from 32 countries and spoke 44 languages.

science.title: Tracking down cellular gene functions with AI and microscopy
science.summary: A new technology promises to enable more comprehensive investigations into how individual genes determine the appearance and behavior of cells. Researchers led by professor Veit Hornung at LMU's Gene Center and professor Matthias Mann at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Martinsried, together with professor Fabian Theis at Helmholtz Munich, have developed SPARCS, a technology that combines artificial intelligence with microscopy and genetic screening.

science.title: Rule gives every generation same share of its best attainable welfare
science.summary: Sharing a finite resource across generations requires a balance between today's needs and the claims of those yet to be born. Research by Prof. Thomas A. Weber, presented at the 2026 European Control Conference in Reykjavík, proposes a fair allocation rule that gives every generation the same fraction of its best attainable welfare. The approach preserves access for all future generations and provides a performance guarantee without requiring agreement on a single social objective.

science.title: Layered semiconductor unlocks magnetic control of light emitted by quantum condensates
science.summary: Quantum technologies are considered key technologies of the future. However, research in this field requires not only scientific expertise but sometimes also highly specialized laboratory conditions. Bose–Einstein condensates are a remarkable example, in which atoms move in lockstep, making quantum-mechanical effects visible not only at the level of individual atoms but also on a macroscopic scale. The first Bose–Einstein condensates were observed in ultracold atomic gases at temperatures close to absolute zero. The cooling required to achieve this was technically demanding, costly and restricted to specialized laboratories.

science.title: Gravity and light reveal how liquids turn into thin fibers
science.summary: From spiders spinning their webs to the manufacturing of textiles, the formation of fibers from liquids plays an important role in both nature and industry. Yet accurately predicting the properties of such fibers remains a challenge. The fiber is often much thinner than the nozzle from which a polymer or solution is extruded. Factors such as temperature, flow conditions and chemical reactions ultimately determine a fiber's thickness and strength.

science.title: 3D-printed inserts bring single-objective light sheet microscopy to commercial sample chambers
science.summary: Light sheet microscopy allows biologists to selectively light up a thin slice of a sample. This method can improve image contrast by reducing background light while remaining gentle on the sample, reducing photodamage and photobleaching. Rice University's Anna-Karin Gustavsson has published a method in Nano Letters that expands the use of light sheet microscopy to work with a single objective in commercially available sample chambers.

science.title: Hearing tests reveal how sea lions and fur seals hear human-made noise
science.summary: Curtin University and Taronga Conservation Society Australia researchers have conducted the first hearing tests on Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals, revealing what sounds these marine mammals can hear and helping assess how human-made noise could affect them.

science.title: NASA Announces Bold Science Initiatives for America’s Golden Age Summit
science.summary: NASA is launching two new science and technology initiatives to deepen scientific understanding and accelerate the innovation that will shape America’s future in space. The initiatives are announced in conjunction with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy’s (OSTP) “Golden Age Summit” in Washington on Thursday with top U.S. agency leaders. The programs […]

science.title: Liquid-crystal-like magnetism explains puzzling properties in a rare-earth compound
science.summary: In some materials, physical properties don't emerge from their individual particles, but from the collective behavior of their quantum spins. Now, researchers led by Pengcheng Dai at Rice University in the U.S. have discovered that in one compound containing the rare-earth element ytterbium, these spins can behave much like the molecules in a liquid crystal: favoring a certain direction without lining up to create magnetism on larger scales.

science.title: Why 'vertical farming' is not a fix for our food system
science.summary: The Canadian government launched its first National Food Security Strategy in June 2026. The strategy aims to invest $750 million to increase year-round Canadian production of fruits and vegetables, including on so-called vertical farms.

science.title: Light-driven method puts notoriously reactive hydrogen atoms to work for chemical synthesis
science.summary: Hydrogen is the simplest element in the periodic table, consisting of just one proton and one electron. In chemistry, however, the smallest of atoms is anything but simple. First produced by Nobel laureate Irving Langmuir over a century ago, single hydrogen atoms (H•) are so reactive that they are almost impossible to prepare and use.

science.title: Are insects really 'poor people's food'?
science.summary: Do people eat insects when there is nothing else to eat? Are insects really "food for the poor" or famine food?

science.title: NASA’s SSPICY Mission to Demonstrate In-Space Inspection Technologies
science.summary: A new NASA-supported spacecraft will get up close to satellites that are no longer in service, demonstrating technologies that could support future in-space repairs and reduce orbital debris. The Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY) mission launched Oct. 1 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. The mission is a technology demonstration where an […]

science.title: Crew-12 Returns to Earth
science.summary: The SpaceX Crew Dragon Freedom spacecraft is seen moments before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California in this Oct. 8, 2026, photograph. Aboard were NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 members NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. The four spent […]

science.title: A trick from tardigrades could help human blood withstand freezing
science.summary: Tardigrades survive conditions that would destroy most other living things: freezing, dehydration and the vacuum of space. Researchers even put tiny tattoos on them, and the animals don't seem to mind. By learning how these critters carry on, researchers hope to find ways to protect human cells.

science.title: Nickel catalyst unlocks hard-to-make β-amino alcohols
science.summary: Many molecules in living organisms and pharmaceuticals share a structure called a β-amino alcohol, in which an amino group and a hydroxyl group sit on neighboring carbon atoms. These groups, important building blocks in biology and medicine, are found in compounds such as sphingosine and ephedrine.

science.title: Fading control over 'jumping genes' may explain why big dogs age faster
science.summary: Across mammals, larger species typically have longer lifespans, ranging from only a couple of years for mice to almost 200 years for some whales.

science.title: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
science.summary: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.

science.title: Mapping how a single cell becomes an entire mouse
science.summary: Growing inside each of us is a cellular family tree. Every one of the 37 trillion cells in our body is generated from another cell, going all the way back to a single fertilized egg. Much like we can draw a family tree tracking generations of our ancestors, scientists can also create family trees of cells, showing how they're related to each other.

science.title: What's your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfillment today
science.summary: In online "prepper" communities—where people discuss ways to prepare for potential emergencies and disruptions—members often jokingly refer to their "zombie apocalypse" skills.

science.title: Webb Measures Distance to Farthest Fast Radio Burst, Suggesting Origin
science.summary: First discovered in 2007, fast radio bursts are enigmatic, millisecond-long flashes of radio emission from the distant universe. Their origin remains uncertain, particularly since most are seen once and never again. Astronomers using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope have pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) seen to date. Their […]

science.title: 'Move away' and 'stop that!' Wild elephants use a rich gestural repertoire intentionally to 'mean business'
science.summary: Wild African savanna elephants use a wide range of gestures when competing with other elephants, according to research from an international group of scientists, including researchers from the University of Portsmouth, University of Vienna and University of St Andrews.

science.title: AI tool makes culturally appropriate lessons for teachers in India
science.summary: Overworked teachers in southern India have a new tool for educating their students: Shiksha Copilot, an AI system that generates culturally relevant lesson plans for schools with few resources.

science.title: All-electrical imaging offers innovative alternative for tracking cell movement
science.summary: Engineers from Brown University have developed a new way of imaging cell migration dynamics that are important in understanding critical processes like cancer metastasis, wound healing and immune response.

science.title: Patience is a lucrative virtue for entrepreneurs, new research finds
science.summary: People with higher levels of patience are more likely to become entrepreneurs and earn more once they do, according to a new study from the University of Bath's School of Management. The researchers analyzed data from more than 21,000 U.K. employees between 2009 and 2023 and found that the most patient individuals were approximately 50% more likely to move into entrepreneurship than the most impatient.

environment.title: Activists cite ecological, social connections in blocking US border wall construction (commentary)
environment.summary: A group of activists in the small border town of Lochiel, Arizona, U.S., is fighting to save 200-year-old cottonwood trees by stopping contractors from building a section of the U.S.’s new wall along its border with Mexico. One activist lived for over 70 days in the upper branches of an ancient cottonwood dubbed the “Grandmother […]

environment.title: Crackdown reveals ‘industrial-scale’ wildlife and timber trafficking across Latin America

Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.

mix_items.summary: An international research effort has examined how children develop the ability to express what story characters think, feel and perceive. Research groups from around the world collected 5,507 picture-based stories from 2,763 typically developing monolingual and bilingual children ages 3 to 13. The children came from 32 countries and spoke 44 languages.

mix_items.title: Tracking down cellular gene functions with AI and microscopy
mix_items.summary: A new technology promises to enable more comprehensive investigations into how individual genes determine the appearance and behavior of cells. Researchers led by professor Veit Hornung at LMU's Gene Center and professor Matthias Mann at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Martinsried, together with professor Fabian Theis at Helmholtz Munich, have developed SPARCS, a technology that combines artificial intelligence with microscopy and genetic screening.

mix_items.title: Rule gives every generation same share of its best attainable welfare
mix_items.summary: Sharing a finite resource across generations requires a balance between today's needs and the claims of those yet to be born. Research by Prof. Thomas A. Weber, presented at the 2026 European Control Conference in Reykjavík, proposes a fair allocation rule that gives every generation the same fraction of its best attainable welfare. The approach preserves access for all future generations and provides a performance guarantee without requiring agreement on a single social objective.

mix_items.title: Understanding adult obesity
mix_items.summary: Obesity is one of the most common health conditions in the world and one of the most misunderstood. Today, it affects about 4 in 10 U.S. adults, and the numbers keep rising.

mix_items.title: Layered semiconductor unlocks magnetic control of light emitted by quantum condensates
mix_items.summary: Quantum technologies are considered key technologies of the future. However, research in this field requires not only scientific expertise but sometimes also highly specialized laboratory conditions. Bose–Einstein condensates are a remarkable example, in which atoms move in lockstep, making quantum-mechanical effects visible not only at the level of individual atoms but also on a macroscopic scale. The first Bose–Einstein condensates were observed in ultracold atomic gases at temperatures close to absolute zero. The cooling required to achieve this was technically demanding, costly and restricted to specialized laboratories.

mix_items.title: Gravity and light reveal how liquids turn into thin fibers
mix_items.summary: From spiders spinning their webs to the manufacturing of textiles, the formation of fibers from liquids plays an important role in both nature and industry. Yet accurately predicting the properties of such fibers remains a challenge. The fiber is often much thinner than the nozzle from which a polymer or solution is extruded. Factors such as temperature, flow conditions and chemical reactions ultimately determine a fiber's thickness and strength.

mix_items.title: 3D-printed inserts bring single-objective light sheet microscopy to commercial sample chambers
mix_items.summary: Light sheet microscopy allows biologists to selectively light up a thin slice of a sample. This method can improve image contrast by reducing background light while remaining gentle on the sample, reducing photodamage and photobleaching. Rice University's Anna-Karin Gustavsson has published a method in Nano Letters that expands the use of light sheet microscopy to work with a single objective in commercially available sample chambers.

mix_items.title: ASTRO: Low-dose radiotherapy shows potential in early knee osteoarthritis
mix_items.summary: Low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) offers multiple benefits in early knee osteoarthritis (OA), according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American Society for Radiation Oncology, held from Sept. 26 to 30 in Boston.

mix_items.title: Hearing tests reveal how sea lions and fur seals hear human-made noise
mix_items.summary: Curtin University and Taronga Conservation Society Australia researchers have conducted the first hearing tests on Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals, revealing what sounds these marine mammals can hear and helping assess how human-made noise could affect them.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover two-pronged strategy to overcome glioblastoma's resistance to immunotherapy
mix_items.summary: Scientists at The Wistar Institute have identified a combination treatment that overcomes two of the biggest barriers to immunotherapy in glioblastoma. In a study published in Neuro-Oncology, the researchers show that reprogramming myeloid cells, a type of immune cell that glioblastoma tumors co-opt to protect themselves, while simultaneously boosting cancer-fighting T cells shrank the tumors and prevented them from coming back.

mix_items.summary: NASA is launching two new science and technology initiatives to deepen scientific understanding and accelerate the innovation that will shape America’s future in space. mix_items.title: The importance of peer support following a termination of pregnancy for medical reasons
mix_items.summary: The first study exploring women's experiences of peer support following a termination for medical reasons (TFMR) highlights the profound isolation, misunderstanding and stigma women experience and the importance of peer support.

mix_items.title: Liquid-crystal-like magnetism explains puzzling properties in a rare-earth compound
mix_items.summary: In some materials, physical properties don't emerge from their individual particles, but from the collective behavior of their quantum spins. Now, researchers led by Pengcheng Dai at Rice University in the U.S. have discovered that in one compound containing the rare-earth element ytterbium, these spins can behave much like the molecules in a liquid crystal: favoring a certain direction without lining up to create magnetism on larger scales.

mix_items.title: Why 'vertical farming' is not a fix for our food system
mix_items.summary: The Canadian government launched its first National Food Security Strategy in June 2026. The strategy aims to invest $750 million to increase year-round Canadian production of fruits and vegetables, including on so-called vertical farms.

mix_items.title: Hospital closures on the rise in both rural and urban areas—particularly among safety-net hospitals
mix_items.summary: More hospitals across the U.S. are closing than opening, and urban hospitals are closing at the same rate as rural ones, according to a new study led by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Further, the hospitals that close are more likely to be those serving socially vulnerable communities.

mix_items.title: Life-course clinical obesity linked to signs of brain health changes in midlife
mix_items.summary: New research from the Bogalusa Heart Study has found that greater exposure to clinical obesity during young adulthood is associated with a greater burden of white matter changes in the brain by midlife, providing new insight into how metabolic health across the life span may influence brain health.

mix_items.title: Light-driven method puts notoriously reactive hydrogen atoms to work for chemical synthesis
mix_items.summary: Hydrogen is the simplest element in the periodic table, consisting of just one proton and one electron. In chemistry, however, the smallest of atoms is anything but simple. First produced by Nobel laureate Irving Langmuir over a century ago, single hydrogen atoms (H•) are so reactive that they are almost impossible to prepare and use.

mix_items.title: A trick from tardigrades could help human blood withstand freezing
mix_items.summary: Tardigrades survive conditions that would destroy most other living things: freezing, dehydration and the vacuum of space. Researchers even put tiny tattoos on them, and the animals don't seem to mind. By learning how these critters carry on, researchers hope to find ways to protect human cells.

mix_items.title: Nickel catalyst unlocks hard-to-make β-amino alcohols
mix_items.summary: Many molecules in living organisms and pharmaceuticals share a structure called a β-amino alcohol, in which an amino group and a hydroxyl group sit on neighboring carbon atoms. These groups, important building blocks in biology and medicine, are found in compounds such as sphingosine and ephedrine.

mix_items.title: Allergic to gold jewelry? Lab tests reveal gold can dissolve from earrings under specific chemical conditions
mix_items.summary: Gold has a reputation for being chemically untouchable. But according to Western University chemist Yolanda Hedberg, that reputation is a little misleading—gold is not unreactive so much as selective about what it reacts with.

mix_items.title: Human milk offers a window into mammary gland function—and its links to infant growth
mix_items.summary: A study led by researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine identified shared molecular patterns in human milk that link maternal nutrition, mammary gland biology and infant growth.

mix_items.title: Fading control over 'jumping genes' may explain why big dogs age faster
mix_items.summary: Across mammals, larger species typically have longer lifespans, ranging from only a couple of years for mice to almost 200 years for some whales.

mix_items.title: Astronomers pinpoint the most distant fast radio burst ever detected
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have detected and traced the most distant fast radio burst ever recorded, a powerful flash of radio waves that traveled for more than 10 billion years across the cosmos before reaching Earth.

mix_items.title: Polynesian wayfinding is written in the genomes of island populations
mix_items.summary: For centuries, Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean, using their knowledge of stars, currents, birds, clouds and the sea to settle islands across the Pacific. Now, a new University of California San Diego study shows the history of voyaging is also reflected in the genomes of Polynesian populations today.

mix_items.title: Mapping how a single cell becomes an entire mouse
mix_items.summary: Growing inside each of us is a cellular family tree. Every one of the 37 trillion cells in our body is generated from another cell, going all the way back to a single fertilized egg. Much like we can draw a family tree tracking generations of our ancestors, scientists can also create family trees of cells, showing how they're related to each other.

mix_items.title: What's your apocalypse skill? Finding a future‑proof hobby can bring fulfillment today
mix_items.summary: In online "prepper" communities—where people discuss ways to prepare for potential emergencies and disruptions—members often jokingly refer to their "zombie apocalypse" skills.

mix_items.summary: Wild African savanna elephants use a wide range of gestures when competing with other elephants, according to research from an international group of scientists, including researchers from the University of Portsmouth, University of Vienna and University of St Andrews.

mix_items.summary: Whether you're struggling with jet lag, working shifts and sleeping during the day, or dealing with more severe insomnia, you might have wondered if melatonin can help you get better sleep.

mix_items.title: AI tool makes culturally appropriate lessons for teachers in India
mix_items.summary: Overworked teachers in southern India have a new tool for educating their students: Shiksha Copilot, an AI system that generates culturally relevant lesson plans for schools with few resources.

mix_items.title: All-electrical imaging offers innovative alternative for tracking cell movement
mix_items.summary: Engineers from Brown University have developed a new way of imaging cell migration dynamics that are important in understanding critical processes like cancer metastasis, wound healing and immune response.

mix_items.title: Patience is a lucrative virtue for entrepreneurs, new research finds
mix_items.summary: People with higher levels of patience are more likely to become entrepreneurs and earn more once they do, according to a new study from the University of Bath's School of Management. The researchers analyzed data from more than 21,000 U.K. employees between 2009 and 2023 and found that the most patient individuals were approximately 50% more likely to move into entrepreneurship than the most impatient.

mix_items.title: PrEP pill can prevent HIV, but partner reactions might stand in the way
mix_items.summary: Fear of accusations of infidelity, the stigma surrounding HIV and concerns about causing conflict in a relationship might deter some Black women from using PrEP, a prescription medicine used to prevent HIV, according to a study led by Rutgers researchers.

mix_items.title: More men living longer with incurable prostate cancer, report finds
mix_items.summary: Men in England diagnosed with incurable advanced prostate cancer are more likely to survive for at least three years than they were a decade ago, according to an analysis by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and partners.

mix_items.title: How political upheaval and the pandemic shaped UK mental health
mix_items.summary: Major societal events such as the Brexit referendum and COVID-19 lockdowns have contributed to a lasting deterioration in mental health in the U.K., a study led by University College London (UCL) researchers finds.

mix_items.title: Personality data reveal link between neuroticism and lasting pandemic anxiety and depression
mix_items.summary: An individual's personality, especially how strongly they react to uncertainty, may help indicate how vulnerable they are to prolonged mental distress during a major crisis, according to a new USC-led study.

mix_items.title: Common herbal sleep aid shows signs of addictive potential
mix_items.summary: Cannabinol is a popular ingredient in over-the-counter sleep products, marketed as a gentle, plant-derived way to unwind at the end of the day. But new research conducted at the University of Connecticut suggests consumers should use it with caution.

mix_items.title: Randomized trial finds targeting individual metastases in oligometastatic breast cancer does not improve survival
mix_items.summary: Treating individual metastatic tumors with highly focused radiation or surgery did not improve progression-free or overall survival for patients with oligometastatic breast cancer receiving first-line systemic therapy, according to results from the randomized NRG-BR002 clinical trial led by researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

mix_items.title: Long-running women's health studies reveal lasting lessons for disease prevention and healthy aging
mix_items.summary: Andrea Romanos-Nanclares, Ph.D., of the Channing Division of Network Medicine within the Department of Medicine at Mass General Brigham, is the lead author of a paper published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health titled "The Nurses' Health Studies: a half-century of discovery in women's health." A. Heather Eliassen, ScD, of Mass General Brigham and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, is the senior author.

mix_items.title: Cervical cancer trial finds similar early recovery results after robot-assisted versus open surgery
mix_items.summary: In early-stage cervical cancer, radical hysterectomy is an established treatment. The operation can be performed either through open surgery or robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery. Until now, there have been limited data from large randomized studies on differences in complications and recovery between the methods.

mix_items.title: Public dataset aims to teach AI to 'show its work' on CT scans
mix_items.summary: Earlier this summer, an international team led by biomedical informatics researchers at Harvard Medical School released the first public dataset that connects descriptive radiological information, such as "3 mm nodule in the lower left lobe," to precise locations in chest CT scans.

mix_items.title: How a new long-acting HIV drug combo tackles resistance
mix_items.summary: A new long-acting HIV treatment could expand options for people who have trouble taking daily pills and whose virus is resistant to some commonly used HIV drugs, according to a new UC San Francisco study.

mix_items.title: New genetic insights could help detect hearing loss earlier
mix_items.summary: A team of hearing specialists at Vanderbilt Health analyzed thousands of data samples in the institution's BioVU biobank to understand genetic susceptibility of sensorineural hearing loss, which is caused by damage to the inner ear. Their study is published in JAMA Otolaryngology-Head & Neck Surgery.

mix_items.title: South Korea strengthens migrant fisher protections. Advocates are not impressed.
mix_items.summary: SEOUL — At 2 a.m. one night, two Indonesian fishers were gripping a flimsy, makeshift rope, hanging on for dear life. The precarious rope dangled from the eighth-floor window of a motel room overlooking a dark alley in the South Korean port city of Busan, swinging left and right with the wind. The men had […]

mix_items.title: Australia’s new eco police flexes muscles with major wildlife trafficking bust
mix_items.summary: Australian authorities have disrupted an alleged wildlife trafficking syndicate, uncovering a clandestine operation where smuggled native animals were hoarded alongside caches of cash and gold, reports contributor Johan Augustin for Mongabay. The operation reportedly seized 28 native and a few exotic species alongside approximately A$300,000 (nearly $210,000) in cash, gold, and silver bullion on July […]

mix_items.title: Ancient viral DNA helps embryonic stem cells grow—and cancer hijacks the same switch
mix_items.summary: Three years ago, George Kassiotis and his team made an unexpected discovery: A specific way of producing a protein called calbindin was found to help cancer cells survive by preventing them from aging. This left Kassiotis, who runs the Crick's Retroviral Immunology Laboratory, confused. Why would a mechanism that boosts cancer growth exist in the first place?

mix_items.title: Scientists outline blueprint for next-generation wearable eye health sensors
mix_items.summary: Dr. Yangzhi Zhu of the Terasaki Institute for Biomedical Innovation (TIBI), with collaborators at UC San Diego and USC, published a Nature Sensors perspective on what it will take to turn tear-based wearable sensors into reliable, long-term health-tracking tools.

mix_items.title: Invasive species have more severe environmental impacts in Global South, study finds
mix_items.summary: The environmental impacts caused by invasive alien species are more severe in poor countries of Global South than wealthy countries of Global North, a new study finds. The study shatters a long-standing assumption that wealthier Global North countries suffer the worst effects of invasive alien species (IAS) and highlights weak governance and insufficient management capacity […]

mix_items.title: Did two of the lemurs stolen in Bangladesh end up in India? Officials are investigating
mix_items.summary: The case of three ring-tailed lemurs, an endangered species, stolen from Gazipur Safari Park in Bangladesh last year resurfaced on social media in September this year, when news spread that two of the lemurs were trafficked to India and later sheltered at a private wildlife conservation facility, Vantara. The viral news prompted Vantara to release […]

mix_items.title: Logging threatens Bornean forest earmarked for Indigenous Peace Park
mix_items.summary: Part of a forest in Malaysian Borneo that Indigenous communities had envisioned co-managing and self-governing has been turned into an active commercial logging concession, according to a recent civil society report. The 283,500-hectare (700,500-acre) Upper Baram Forest Area, in the northeastern part of the state of Sarawak, was proposed as a community-led conservation area more […]

mix_items.title: Traumatic brain injury can alter the brain's subsequent response to stress, study shows
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Department of Cell Biology, Genetics and Physiology at the University of Malaga have led an international scientific team studying how a traumatic brain injury caused by a severe blow to the head affects the brain's long-term response to subsequent stressful situations.

mix_items.title: Just 7 days of strength training started shrinking fat cells in mice
mix_items.summary: Just seven strength-training sessions helped obese mice shrink visceral fat cells and reactivate molecular pathways involved in burning stored fat, despite no change in overall body weight. The findings suggest some benefits of resistance exercise may begin long before weight loss becomes visible, though the results still need to be confirmed in humans.

mix_items.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
mix_items.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.
